compensating.why: hop 3 treats a kept set at least as large as the list's set as keeping every element
hop 4 also clears an empty list directly
hop 2 gathers the elements to keep in the collection's order

expected_signature: Collection size should match confirmed collection's expected:<3> but was:<10>
ownership_reason: Only the gold walks the list and decides, position by position, whether the element there stays: hops 1 and 2 hold the collection and the list's set and gather the elements to keep, hop 3 compares the size of that set with the list's set and hop 4 chooses between clearing the list and the removal pass; none of them sees a position. Once the pass has gone over an element without examining it, a caller can take it out only by running a removal of its own over the list. The gold's javadoc promises that the elements not in the given set are removed from the list and the others keep their order. The convention that a removal pass examines every element, including the one that moves into the place of a removed element, is pinned outside the gold: CollectionUtils.filter removes every element its predicate rejects, visiting each through the iterator (CollectionUtilsTest filter removes both adjacent 3s of [1, 2, 3, 3] and passes); the bidi map views' in-place retainAll (AbstractDualBidiMap.View) walks its iterator and removes every element the collection lacks; ListUtils.retainAll keeps exactly the elements the other collection contains, in order (ListUtilsTest testRetainAll); SetUniqueList.removeAll removes every named element; the same testCollectionRetainAll passes for TreeList, and SetUniqueListTest testRetainAll pins the facade's result on 0..9.
